question.text: Google's AlphaQubit spots errors in a quantum chip more accurately than the hand-written decoders. But it never looks at the qubits doing the actual work. So what is it reading?
options: The data qubits themselves, measured at the end of every correction round
The control pulses going into the chip, checked for distortion
Syndrome measurements — parity checks from helper qubits that reveal an error happened without revealing the data
The final output, compared against a known-correct answer
question.hint: You can't examine the patient without killing them. So you read the chart instead.

explain.g: Measuring a data qubit destroys the superposition you were trying to protect — so error correction never touches them. Instead, extra 'helper' qubits ask a question that gives nothing away: do these two neighbours still agree? The pattern of yes/no answers is the syndrome, and it tells you that something broke and roughly where, while the data itself stays untouched and unread. AlphaQubit reads that pattern. Symptoms, not the disease.
explain.y: Each helper qubit measures a parity check — a joint property of several data qubits, never any single one. Because those checks are chosen to commute with the logical information, learning their outcomes collapses nothing you care about: you find out that an error occurred without finding out what state you were holding. The decoder's job is inverse inference — given this syndrome pattern over many rounds, which physical error most likely produced it? Note what AlphaQubit's win actually is: it is an accuracy win, and it is measured against specific opponents. Roughly 30% versus correlated matching, the fast real-time class; only about 6% versus the most accurate tensor-network decoder. It is also, as published, too slow for the real-time loop.
explain.r: The surface code fixes a stabilizer group S of commuting Pauli operators; the codespace is their simultaneous +1 eigenspace. Measuring a generator S_i projects onto its ±1 eigenspace, and because every S_i commutes with the logical operators X̄ and Z̄, that projection leaves the encoded state undisturbed — the syndrome carries information about the error coset, not about the logical state. An error E anticommuting with S_i flips that check, so the syndrome is the map E ↦ (±1)^m, which is many-to-one: distinct errors differing by a stabilizer are indistinguishable and, correctly, need no distinguishing. Decoding is choosing the most likely coset, and it is degenerate maximum-likelihood, not simple error identification. AlphaQubit is a recurrent-transformer decoder pretrained on hundreds of millions of simulated samples and fine-tuned on thousands of experimental samples from a Sycamore processor at distance 3 and 5 (Google DeepMind, Nature 635, 834 (2024); arXiv 2310.05900). Surface-code background: Fowler, Mariantoni, Martinis & Cleland, arXiv 1208.0928.

signal: AlphaQubit's edge is accuracy, not speed — the real-time decoding problem is being solved separately, by FPGAs (arXiv 2605.04892: 550 ns system latency inside a 1.25 μs cycle).
